source: Weir, Chappell, Kacelnik (2002) Shaping of hooks in New Caledonian crows. Science 297:981
finding: Captive crow Betty chose between a hooked and a straight wire to lift a small bucket of meat from a vertical tube. On trial 5 her mate Abel took the hook. Betty wedged the straight wire under tape, bent it into a hook with her beak, and got the food. The authors called it the first new tool made for a specific task without a long period of trial and error.
numbers: Bending first seen on trial 5 of the choice test. Later, with only straight wire, she repeatedly made hooks by several techniques (trials 7 and 13 are the example videos). N=1 bird. The '9 of 10 retrievals' figure is from Wikipedia only and was NOT verified in the paper.
limits: N=1, one accidental first event, wild-caught adult with unknown history. Original is a one-page Brevia (page read is the Oxford group summary, not the paper). Later field work shows wild crows bend stems routinely, so 'novel invention' is contested.
agent_relevance: Anchor case for making a missing tool to a need. The agent should be able to build a missing helper when the stock one is gone, then test it on the same task. One lucky success does not prove the rule behind it (G3).

source: Kacelnik interview, Reflections on Papers Past (2018) Revisiting Weir et al. 2002
finding: Kacelnik recalls the event. Abel took the hooked wire, leaving Betty only straight wire. She jammed it at the base of the tube and bent it. No experimenter intervened. The long paper was cut to a Brevia on the editor's advice. Betty also took a wire away, made the hook elsewhere and came back, which Kacelnik reads as working memory. Rooks later solved a similar problem but pulled the wire over the tube edge.
numbers: Betty died of aspergillosis aged about 6. A crow vs kea comparison across four tasks: crows better at tool use, keas more flexible.
quote: the use of physical materials as tools is exceptionally well developed
limits: Retrospective interview, no new data. Kacelnik cautions crows are not exceptional on all cognitive dimensions.
agent_relevance: The key evidence was one unplanned observation that was then re-created under control. Same rule as ours: an observed success needs a deliberate re-run before it counts.

source: Weir and Kacelnik (2006) A New Caledonian crow creatively re-designs tools by bending or unbending aluminium strips. Anim Cogn 9:317-334
finding: Betty was given novel aluminium strips in three experiments. She first tried her old wedge-under-tape method, it failed, and she changed only one step (bending the end with her beak while the strip stayed wedged). When unbending was needed she adjusted the material correctly on 4 of 5 trials. She did not bend when bending was counter-productive.
numbers: N=1 bird, 3 experiments, 4/5 correct modification when unbending was required. Per the van Buuren review: unbending task 1 was inconclusive; in task 2 she unbent on trials 3 and 4, then died.
limits: Single subject. The authors say probing with unmodified tools and using the unsuitable end after modifying argue against full understanding or planning. Only the abstract page was read.
agent_relevance: Goal-directed repair: change one step of a failing procedure and keep the rest. Fits revision from real failing output (G2), not wholesale restart.

source: van Buuren, Alfredsson, Mioduszewska, Tebbich, von Bayern (2021) Bending and unbending of tools by New Caledonian crows in a problem-solving context. Anim Behav Cogn 8(2):190-215
finding: Largest controlled follow-up to Betty: 17 captive crows, one bending task and three unbending tasks. Study 1: two groups of 5 were trained on rigid straight or rigid hooked tools, then given the wrong type but pliable. Three made hooks and one straightened tools consistently. Study 2: 13 crows (5 from study 1); 10 got a Z-shaped tool needing two straightenings. Four solved it at least once and two did consistently. One crow succeeded in both unbending tasks consistently. Authors conclude trial-and-error learning prevailed.
numbers: 17 crows total. Study 1: 3 of 10 made hooks, 1 straightened consistently. Study 2: 4 of 10 solved at least once, 2 consistently. Follow-up apparatus: 8 birds tested, 1 consistent in both tasks.
limits: Partial replication: the capacity exists in more than one bird but only a minority solve. Mechanisms differed between birds. Data were collected before the field finding that bending is natural, so predisposition cannot be ruled out.
agent_relevance: Replication rate is low (about 30-40% of birds, 1 of 17 across every task). A tool-making step in our agent will work on some problems and not others; measure it, do not assume it.

source: van Buuren et al. (2021), background on criticism of Weir et al. 2002 and field data
finding: Critique: the first bend may simply have been the first manipulation tried and then reinforced; Shettleworth (2009) said shaping could not be excluded. Field work (Klump et al. 2015; Rutz et al. 2016) shows wild crows routinely bend the shaft of hook tools: 10 of 18 temporarily captive wild crows bent the shaft of a newly crafted hook, mostly holding it with the feet and bending with the beak, or wedging it upright and pulling sideways (as Betty did).
numbers: 10 of 18 wild crows bent the shaft (Klump et al. 2015, as cited by van Buuren).
limits: Second-hand: Klump 2015 and Rutz 2016 were not opened.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation to flag: apparent invention can be an inherited or earlier-learned routine. When our agent seems to invent a tool, check whether it is retrieving a known pattern before counting it as novel (G8).

source: Kenward, Weir, Rutz, Kacelnik (2005) Tool manufacture by naive juvenile crows. Nature 433:121
finding: Four hand-raised New Caledonian crows kept away from adults spontaneously used and made tools. Two had a human foster parent demonstrate twig tool use; two never saw tool use. Authors saw no qualitative difference and argued for an inherited predisposition.
numbers: N=4 hand-raised juveniles; 2 tutored, 2 untutored (from search summaries, not full text).
limits: Not opened (search summaries only). N=4. The 2006 follow-up shows social demonstration did change the amount of tool handling.
agent_relevance: Tool making can come from a built-in prior, not only from learning. A seeded starter library plays that role for our agent.

source: Kenward, Rutz, Weir, Kacelnik (2006) Development of tool use in New Caledonian crows: inherited action patterns and social influences. Anim Behav 72:1329-1343
finding: Four hand-reared captive-bred chicks. Successful food retrieval was preceded by stereotyped object manipulation patterns resembling parts of the adult behaviour, so tool-oriented behaviour is an evolved specialisation. Juveniles that saw twig-tool demonstrations handled and inserted twigs more and preferred objects they had seen manipulated. Authors: inherited patterns, individual learning, social transmission and creative problem solving all contribute.
numbers: N=4 chicks, 2 given demonstrations and 2 naive; demonstrations ran until about 51 days after leaving the nest; 'protoprobing' is a defined precursor action in the ethogram.
limits: Very small N. The social effect is on how much handling occurs, not on whether tool use appears.
agent_relevance: A tool library works best as seed (inherited), experience (learned) and shared examples (social). Supports shipping a starter set and letting the agent add to it.

source: Hunt (2000) Human-like, population-level specialization in the manufacture of pandanus tools by New Caledonian crows. Proc R Soc B 267
finding: In wild crows, pandanus leaf hook tools show population-level handedness and shaping to a rule system. Hunt says these features are unprecedented in free-living non-humans and are not tied to symbolic thought or language.
numbers: Abstract page only; tool counts not read.
limits: Only the abstract page was read, not the paper.
agent_relevance: Tools made to a standard pattern show that making can be rule-governed. A library entry should record the rule it was built by, so it can be rebuilt.

source: Hunt (1996) Manufacture and use of hook-tools by New Caledonian crows. Nature 379:249-251
finding: First report of free-living non-human hook tool use: a hooked twig and a stepped-cut barbed pandanus leaf, both made and used to catch prey.
numbers: No figures read this session.
limits: Not opened; known from a search snippet and secondary citations.
agent_relevance: Origin of the 'hook and stepped tool made to a standard' idea in the subfield row.

source: Emery and Clayton (2004) The mentality of crows: convergent evolution of intelligence in corvids and apes. Science 306:1903-1907
finding: Review of wild and lab crow tool behaviour. Hook tools are made from twigs by trimming and sculpting and used with slow deliberate movements. Stepped-cut Pandanus tools are made to a standardised pattern and carried on foraging trips; manufacture is lateralised at population level. The number of steps in stepped tools may grow over time (cumulative evolution), and tool types differ between populations independent of ecology.
numbers: Cites Betty modifying novel wire into a hook (ref 21) and choosing the right length or diameter from a tool box (refs 22, 23).
quote: complex cognition depends on a ``tool kit'' consisting of causal reasoning, flexibility, imagination, and prospection
limits: A review, so claims are only as strong as the cited studies. The cognitive 'tool kit' is: causal reasoning, flexibility, imagination, prospection.
agent_relevance: Source of the 'tool kit' framing. For us the helper set should cover causal reasoning, flexibility, imagination and planning, not only calculators.

source: Emery and Clayton (2004) The mentality of crows: convergent evolution of intelligence in corvids and apes. Science 306:1903-1907 (theory)
finding: Theory: corvids and apes evolved similar cognition independently (convergent evolution) despite very different brains. Betty is read as reasoning by analogy from earlier hook experience; her wire hook 'suggests some appreciation of mechanical causation' and corvid tool use goes beyond simple associative processes. The authors concede the role of basic instrumental conditioning in wild tool use is unclear.
numbers: No test of its own; rests on single-bird Betty data (N=1).
quote: suggests some appreciation of mechanical causation
limits: The interpretation went beyond the data in 2004. Later work (Taylor 2012; van Buuren 2021) favours simpler mechanisms in many cases. No formal or computational model of tool manufacture exists in this literature; only verbal accounts (insight, feedback loop, inherited template).
agent_relevance: Be careful with analogy claims: an agent reusing a tool across tasks is not evidence it knows why the tool works. Verify transfer by running (G3).

source: Bird and Emery (2009) Insightful problem solving and creative tool modification by captive nontool-using rooks. PNAS 106:10370
finding: Four hand-raised captive rooks, a species that does not use tools in the wild, all bent straight wire into a hook and used it to lift the bucket. Three of 4 did so on the first trial and the fourth by trial 4.
numbers: N=4 rooks. A hook was made on every trial but the bucket was retrieved on 35 +/- 2.9% of trials. Successful hooks had a bend of 100 +/- 8.5 degrees, unsuccessful 75 +/- 4.5; Betty's successful range was 74 +/- 30. Two occasions (5% of trials) succeeded by stabbing the bucket with straight wire. Functional-hook choice: 3 of 4 on trial 1, the fourth from trial 3.
limits: N=4 hand-raised captive birds with earlier tool tests. Authors argue the ability is domain-general. Kacelnik's PNAS commentary asks whether 'insight' is needed to explain it.
agent_relevance: Making a tool is possible without a tool-using lineage; a general causal model is enough. Supports a general mechanism over a pile of special recipes.

source: Bird and Emery (2009), stone, tool choice and metatool tests
finding: Rooks chose a suitable stone size, picked functional tools on the first trial, and solved a metatool task. All 4 solved the metatool task from trial 1.
numbers: N=4. 3 of 4 chose the medium or large stone on trial 1 without trying others first; 3 of 4 rotated a stone into the right orientation on trial 1 and 2 did so without first trying horizontal; all 4 chose functional tools on trial 1 in both choice tests.
limits: N=4. First-trial performance is the strong evidence; later trials could reflect learning.
agent_relevance: First-trial success is the right test for a library: judge a tool on first use on an unseen item, not after tuning.

source: Taylor, Knaebe, Gray (2012) An end to insight? New Caledonian crows can spontaneously solve problems without planning their actions. Proc R Soc B 279:4977
finding: Failed replication of the insight reading of string pulling. Humans passed a novel horizontal string-pulling task. Crows did not: no individual preferred the connected string and all but one never got the food even once. Authors conclude string pulling is a perceptual-motor feedback loop, not planning.
numbers: Humans: 49/50 (experiment 1) and 42/50 (experiment 2) correct, p<0.00001. Crows: 8/11 chose the connected string on trial 1 (p=0.11); one crow finished 20 trials at 13/20 (p=0.13); others made a choice in 2.5 +/- 0.6 trials then stopped; group 16/25 (p=0.11); pooled p=0.037, which the authors treat as possibly a fluke.
limits: Tests string pulling, not tool manufacture, but it is the main 'no insight' result against the same family of claims. Only 11 crows and nearly all disengaged.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous success can come from tight perception-action loops, not a model. A right tool choice is not evidence of an internal plan. Prefer outcome checks (G10).

source: Gruber, Schiestl, Boeckle, Frohnwieser, Miller, Gray, Clayton, Taylor (2019) New Caledonian crows use mental representations to solve metatool problems. Curr Biol 29:686
finding: Strongest evidence for planning with tools. Wild-caught crows faced metatool problems where each stage was out of sight, with a distractor tool or apparatus. Experiment 1 (N=14; 11 got the stick problem first): 4 reached 16/20 with few errors, 3 more within 40 trials, 1 at trial 43. Experiment 2 (N=8, with a shortcut condition): 3 solved within 60 trials (25, 26, 39 trials), a 4th at 69. Experiment 3 (N=3, apparatus identity swapped): all 3 passed the stick condition in 20 trials (18, 17, 16 of 20), none passed the stone condition in 20 and only one in 60.
numbers: Exp 1 stone problem: 2 reached criterion within 40 trials, 2 more at trials 43 and 46. Three crows given the stone problem first failed within 40 trials, then reached stick criterion in 22, 23, 24 trials.
quote: This provides the first conclusive evidence that birds can plan several moves ahead while using tools.
limits: Crows needed tens of trials, so not one-shot insight. Stone condition was much harder than stick (asymmetry). Birds were wild-caught and tested in field aviaries.
agent_relevance: Even successful tool chaining needs many trials and works more in one direction. Plan a chain of helper calls only when each stage can be checked, and budget for retries (G12).

source: Gruber et al. (2019), design logic and hypotheses
finding: Two competing accounts are pitted against each other: mental representation of goals and sub-goals (Dennett's 'Popperian creatures', whose hypotheses 'die in their stead') versus chaining with perceptual-motor feedback. If the feedback account is right, crows should fail when stages are out of sight and distractors are present. The shortcut trial tests whether the final goal is represented.
numbers: Design: distractor tool or apparatus in every problem; shortcut trial type; stick and stone conditions are mirror images.
limits: Verbal explanatory model, not a computational one.
agent_relevance: A concrete test for the agent: put distractor helpers in the library and check it picks the one that serves the goal, not the nearest one.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Holzhaider, Gray (2007) Spontaneous metatool use by New Caledonian crows. Curr Biol 17:1504-1507
finding: Seven wild-caught crows were given a short stick that could extract a longer stick, which could then reach meat. Six of 7 tried to extract the long tool with the short one and four got meat on the first trial. Authors argued for analogical reasoning, not trial and error.
numbers: N=7; 6 of 7 attempted; 4 of 7 succeeded on trial 1 (from a search summary; PDF returned 403).
limits: Not opened. Gruber 2019 later showed that this success needed tens of trials once stages were hidden.
agent_relevance: Core pattern of a tool used to get a tool, the animal template for helpers that fetch other helpers.

source: Chappell and Kacelnik (2002, 2004) Tool selection in New Caledonian crows (as cited by Emery and Clayton 2004)
finding: Betty chose tools of the right length or diameter from a tool box to reach food. Seen only as a citation in the Emery and Clayton review.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand; primary papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Choosing the right-size tool from a box is the animal form of library retrieval by fit to the task.

source: Cai, Wang, Ma, Chen, Zhou (2023; ICLR 2024) Large Language Models as Tool Makers (LATM)
finding: Two stages: a strong LLM (GPT-4) makes a reusable Python tool once per task type, and a cheap LLM (GPT-3.5 Turbo) uses it. A dispatcher decides whether an existing tool fits or a new one must be made. With the tool, GPT-3.5 Turbo matched GPT-4 with chain of thought on six tasks.
numbers: GPT-3.5 Turbo CoT -> LATM: Logical Deduction 66.4 -> 79.7; Tracking Shuffled Objects 61.6 -> 99.6; Dyck 20.4 -> 92.2; Word Sorting 59.2 -> 98.3; Chinese Remainder Theorem 0.0 -> 100.0; Schedule Meeting 18.9 -> 100.0. GPT-4 as user, CoT vs LATM: 88.8/86.6, 100/100, 63.6/87.5, 90.9/99.1, 0/100, 55.6/100 (same task order). Dispatcher picks the right existing tool 95% +/- 2% and correctly requests tool-making for unseen tasks 96% +/- 3%.
limits: Six tasks that suit short programs. GPT-3.5 Turbo as maker failed all 5 trials on Logical Deduction and Tracking Shuffled Objects because its tool only fit the training samples. The verification stage fixed the tool from error messages in only 2 of 60 trials. On Dyck, GPT-3.5 as user beat GPT-4 as user because GPT-4 over-edited the argument.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a helper library: make once, reuse many times, route by a small dispatcher. Warning: a tool that fits only the examples is the G3 failure, so test on held-out items.

source: Cai et al. LATM, tool-user capacity ablation (Table 4)
finding: Using the same GPT-4-made tools, weaker user models fall off fast. Order of users: GPT-3.5 Turbo, text-davinci-002, davinci, curie, babbage, ada.
numbers: Rows identified by the GPT-3.5 Turbo value (equal to its Table 2 LATM score), users in the order above: Logical Deduction 79.7 / 58.2 / 11.6 / 6.5 / 11.6 / 3.0; Tracking Shuffled Objects 99.6 / 100 / 62.1 / 20.7 / 16.4 / 5.2; Dyck 92.2 / 35.8 / 16.4 / 18.1 / 9.1 / 9.9; Word Sorting 98.3 / 60.8 / 26.6 / 7.3 / 7.3 / 0.9; the last two rows (Chinese Remainder Theorem and Schedule Meeting, both 100 for GPT-3.5) are 100 / 100 / 99.6 / 93.1 / 75.0 / 66.0 and 100 / 100 / 62.9 / 59.1 / 23.2 / 0.0 in unclear order
limits: Table layout in the extracted text was slightly scrambled; the printed row labels were offset by one in the extracted text, so rows were matched by value to Table 2.
agent_relevance: A shared library only helps if the user model can call tools correctly. Test the calling step on its own.

source: Qian, Han, Fung, Qin, Liu, Ji (2023) CREATOR: Tool creation for disentangling abstract and concrete reasoning of LLMs
finding: Four stages: creation (write a tool with docs), decision (plan the call), execution, rectification (fix from errors). Separating abstract creation from concrete use beat the entangled version. Rectification adds about 10% of the original accuracy.
numbers: ChatGPT: MATH 59.7%, TabMWP 94.7%, Creation Challenge (2K questions) 75.5%. TabMWP no-CoT / with-CoT: standard 68.2/75.2, program-of-thought with rectification 81.2/87.3, tool use 77.6/79.6, CREATOR-Entangled 91.6/93.5, CREATOR 90.5/94.7. Creation Challenge hints: none 63.8, utility hint 67.2, all hint 75.7. Rectification lifts PoT on TabMWP from 80.0 to 87.3.
limits: Chain of thought conflicts with code on hard MATH problems. Hints about what the tool should do lifted Creation Challenge accuracy by up to 18.7% (paper text).
agent_relevance: Matches G2: revision from a real error message gives a reliable gain. Keep 'design the helper' separate from 'use the helper'.

source: Qian et al. (2023) CREATOR, tool transfer experiment
finding: 100 sets of three problems share a core concept but differ in scenario. A tool made for one scenario was reused on the other two. Accuracy rose from 63.0% to 78.3% (+15.3 points). 39 sets improved and 2 got worse. The paper also names three levels of tool creation: enhancing an existing tool, chaining several tools, and building a new one.
numbers: 100 sets, 300 data pieces, ChatGPT as base.
limits: Only tools already judged correct were transferred, so this is an upper estimate of transfer.
agent_relevance: Transfer of a verified tool across scenarios is the main payoff of a library, but only for tools already verified.

source: Yuan, Chen, Wang, Fung, Peng, Ji (2023; ICLR 2024) CRAFT: customizing LLMs by creating and retrieving from specialized toolsets
finding: Build a task-specific toolset from solved training examples (GPT-4 solves, check, abstract into generic snippets, deduplicate). At test time retrieve snippets and write code that calls them. No finetuning.
numbers: Average 43.16% relative F1 gain over best baselines on vision-language tasks. GPT-3.5-Turbo, SAcc/F1: GQA vanilla ViperGPT 35.0/36.9, LATM 29.4/30.3, CREATOR 34.3/38.4, CRAFT 45.4/48.8; OK-VQA vanilla 15.4/24.7, LATM 7.8/11.8, CREATOR 16.7/27.3, CRAFT 33.4/43.0; A-OKVQA vanilla 15.6/23.0, CRAFT 30.8/40.6. TabMWP accuracy: CoT 75.2, vanilla 80.6, CREATOR 81.0, BM25 retrieval 89.2, CRAFT 88.4.
limits: BM25 retrieval matched or beat CRAFT on TabMWP because its patterns are simple. LATM scored below vanilla on VQA. MATH-algebra numbers were not used because the extracted table was scrambled.
agent_relevance: Build the library from solved, checked examples and retrieve by fit. One tool per task (LATM) lost to a larger abstracted toolset on VQA.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) CRAFT, ablations and scaling
finding: Removing the abstraction step lowers performance on all three VQA sets, though even the un-abstracted toolset still beats ViperGPT. Performance keeps rising with more tools and with a stronger backbone. Math has the most varied patterns, then VQA, while TabMWP is homogeneous and well solved by few tools.
numbers: GPT-4 backbone, SAcc/F1 on GQA: ViperGPT 51.4/53.7 vs CRAFT 55.6/58.8. Absolute SAcc gains over ViperGPT with GPT-3.5: +10.4 GQA, +18.0 OK-VQA, +15.2 A-OKVQA.
limits: Per-ablation rows for function name, docstring and problem text could not be read reliably from the extracted table; only the direction is firm (each removal lowers results).
agent_relevance: Library entries need clear names and docstrings because retrieval keys on them. Each entry should carry a one-line contract.

source: Wang, Xie, Jiang, Mandlekar, Xiao, Zhu, Fan, Anandkumar (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: A GPT-4 agent in Minecraft stores working action programs in a skill library (vector database keyed by description embedding) and builds new skills on old ones. It found 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x more than baselines, travelled 2.3x further, and unlocked wooden / stone / iron tools 15.3x / 8.5x / 6.4x faster. Only Voyager reached diamond.
numbers: Zero-shot to new tasks in a fresh world (3 trials, 50 iteration cap): Voyager 19+/-3, 18+/-7, 21+/-5, 18+/-2 iterations for diamond pickaxe, golden sword, lava bucket, compass, all 3/3. Without the skill library: 2/3, 3/3, 3/3, 3/3 and slower (36, 30, 27, 26). ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGPT: 0/3 on all four. AutoGPT with Voyager's library: 1/3, 1/3, 0/3, 2/3. Random curriculum cut discovered items by 93%.
limits: The library alone is not enough without the curriculum and self-verification. The no-library variant plateaus late rather than failing. Minecraft only; GPT-4 black box.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analog of an accumulating tool kit: stored code skills are reusable, compose, and help other agents. A skill enters only after self-verification confirms the task is done (G3).

source: Schick, Dwivedi-Yu, Dessi, Raileanu, Lomeli, Zettlemoyer, Cancedda, Scialom (2023) Toolformer: language models can teach themselves to use tools
finding: A 6.7B model (GPT-J) is finetuned on its own API calls (calculator, Q&A, search, translation, calendar), kept only if the call lowers loss on later tokens. Zero-shot it beats much larger models on facts and arithmetic.
numbers: LAMA (SQuAD / Google-RE / T-REx): Toolformer 33.8 / 11.5 / 53.5 vs GPT-3 175B 26.8 / 7.0 / 39.8; gains of 11.7, 5.2 and 18.6 points over the best same-size baseline; it used the Q&A tool in 98.1% of cases. Math (ASDiv / SVAMP / MAWPS): Toolformer 40.4 / 29.4 / 44.0 vs GPT-3 14.0 / 10.0 / 19.8, OPT 66B 6.0 / 4.9 / 7.9, Toolformer with calls disabled 14.8 / 6.3 / 15.0, GPT-J 7.5 / 5.2 / 9.9. Calculator used on 97.9% of examples. One call per input at most.
limits: Tool USE learned by finetuning, not tool making. Fixed set of tools, one call per input, no chains. Lenient scoring (answer within first 5 words; first number for math). Row assignment in the extracted tables was reconstructed from the text.
agent_relevance: A call to a fixed tool is cheap and strong for known sub-steps. A call that lowers later error is a usable keep rule for library entries.

source: Xu, Huang, Yu, Liu, Zhang, Niu, Zhang, Xia, Tan, Zhao (2023) Creative robot tool use with large language models (RoboTool)
finding: RoboTool turns instructions into robot code with four LLM parts: Analyzer, Planner, Calculator, Coder. Six tasks cannot be done without using objects as tools. Examples: a hammer used as an L-shaped handle (Milk-Reaching), a 15-step plan (Can-Grasping), a lever built from a surfboard and a yoga roller (Cube-Lifting, quadruped).
numbers: Real-world success was 0.1 below simulation but still above every simulated baseline. Removing the Analyzer or the Calculator lowered success; the Calculator mattered most on tasks needing exact positional offsets.
limits: Only the narrative results were read, not the success-rate table. Perception and execution errors cause the real-world drop.
agent_relevance: Built on the animal tool-use literature. An LLM can pick an object for a non-standard use from its properties, but numeric offsets should come from code (G1, G5).

source: Wolflein, Ferber, Truhn, Arandjelovic, Kather (2025) LLM agents making agent tools (ToolMaker)
finding: An agent turns a paper plus GitHub repo into a callable tool: installs dependencies, writes code and self-corrects in a closed loop. On 15 computational tasks with over 100 unit tests it implemented 80% (12 of 15) correctly vs 20% (3 of 15) for OpenHands with gpt-4o.
numbers: 12/15 vs 3/15. One multi-step tool (a STAMP classifier) took 9 self-correcting iterations and 33 actions. Cost about $0.94 per tool for ToolMaker.
limits: Life-science and medical tasks; tests written by the authors. One task (esm_fold_predict) was only partly correct.
agent_relevance: Unit tests are the gate for entering the library (G2, G3). The self-correction loop keyed to real failing output is the part that works.

source: Wang, Neubig, Fried (2024) TroVE: inducing verifiable and efficient toolboxes for solving programmatic tasks. ICML
finding: Training-free toolbox induction by using, growing and periodically trimming functions. Across 11 datasets (math, table QA, image reasoning) it gives simpler solutions with higher accuracy than primitive-only baselines and prior tool-making methods, with 79-98% smaller toolboxes.
numbers: 79-98% smaller toolboxes; human verification 31% faster and 13% more accurate than baselines; 11 datasets.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read; per-dataset accuracies were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Trim the library: a small verified set beats a large noisy one. Adds a prune step to the make-and-use loop.
